papers.title: Fine-Grained Complexity Across the Computational Phase Transition
papers.abstract: How does a computational problem transition from easy to hard? In the hard-core model, approximate counting and sampling are polynomial-time tractable up to tree uniqueness, but worst-case intractable at any constant relative distance above it unless $\mathsf{NP}=\mathsf{RP}$. We quantify the transition from polynomial to exponential mixing for classical Glauber dynamics. On $n$-vertex graphs of maximum degree $d\ge3$, at fugacity $λ=(1+δ)λ_{\mathrm c}(d)$ with sufficiently small $δ\ge0$ that may vanish with $n$, its worst-case mixing time has the form $\exp\{Θ(nδ^2/d)\}n^{1+Θ(1)}$. The upper bound is degree-uniform, and the matching lower bound holds for every fixed $d$. Annealing gives approximate counting with the same running-time upper bound at fixed accuracy. For general sampling and counting algorithms, we establish a robust fine-grained reduction from SAT without assuming a lower bound on SAT's running time. For any fixed $d\ge3$ and $0<γ<1$, a sampling or approximate-counting algorithm running in $\exp\{O((nδ^2/d)^{1-γ})\}\operatorname{poly}(n)$ time along any one suitable inverse-polynomial distance sequence $δ=δ(n)$, yields a randomized SAT algorithm running in $\exp\{\widetilde O(s^{1-γ})\}$ time on inputs of binary length $s$. This power-saving transfer identifies $nδ^2/d$ as the analogue of SAT input length for hard-core sampling and counting at relative distance $δ$ above criticality: beating the Glauber exponent by a fixed power through any sampling or counting method would yield a corresponding power improvement for SAT. At criticality, we establish $O(\sqrt{n/d})$ spectral independence, optimal in $n$ at fixed degree, and degree-uniform Glauber mixing in $\widetilde O(n(n/d)^{1+1/(d-2)})$ time, improving the previous $\widetilde O(n^{4+4/(d-2)})$ bound.

papers.title: Reed-Muller Codes are Optimal Binary Linear 3-Query LCCs
papers.abstract: We prove that any linear $3$-query locally correctable code $C \colon \mathbb{F}_2^k \to \mathbb{F}_2^n$ with constant correction radius must have length $n \geq 2^{Ω(\sqrt{k})}$. This improves on the prior best lower bound of $2^{Ω(\sqrt{k/\log k})}$, due to [AG24], and shows that the folklore construction of linear $3$-LCCs from Reed-Muller codes, which achieve length $n = 2^{O(\sqrt{k})}$, is optimal up to constant factors in the exponent. Our proof builds on the approach of [KM24a], further refined in [Yan24,KM24b], that uses "chain derived equations" in combination with Kikuchi graphs. The crux of our argument is to show that a certain edge-coloured Kikuchi graph has a unique colour cycle: a cycle in which some colour is used exactly once. We do this by controlling the distribution of colours at each vertex in the graph using a random walk mixing argument and a novel hypergraph decomposition based on edge expansion of the hypergraph's "flattening" into a graph.

papers.title: Hardness Results for Approximate Distance Labeling in Sparse Graphs
papers.abstract: Distance labeling schemes assign short labels to the vertices of a graph so that distances between pairs of vertices can be recovered, exactly or approximately, from the two corresponding labels alone. For sparse graphs, Kosowski, Uznański, and Viennot [PODC'2019] showed that, assuming the hardness of the Sum-Index communication problem, exact distance labeling for sparse unweighted graphs requires near-linear label size. Their construction also gives lower bounds for stretch $1+o(1)$, but does not rule out substantially smaller labels for stretch $1+\varepsilon$, where $\varepsilon>0$ is fixed. We prove lower bounds for this $(1+\varepsilon)$-stretch regime through a density/stretch tradeoff. For every constant integer $k\ge 1$, we show that any approximate distance labeling scheme with stretch strictly smaller than $1+1/k$ for unweighted graphs with $m=O(n^{1+1/k})$ edges requires maximum label size at least $\mathrm{SumIndex}(n)/2^{O_k(\sqrt{\log n})}$ for infinitely many values of $n$. Thus, under the conjecture that $\mathrm{SumIndex}(n)=n^{1-o(1)}$, the maximum label size must be $n^{1-o(1)}$. The main new ingredient is an unweighted graph construction based on $3$-AP-free sets, which replaces the weighted uniqueness mechanism of the previous Sum-Index reduction by an additive uniqueness mechanism and keeps the relevant critical paths short enough to obtain a constant multiplicative distance gap. The same construction also yields near-tight lower bounds for related $2$-hop structures, including hub labeling schemes, shortcut sets, and approximate distance hopsets.

papers.title: Worst-Case to Average-Case Reductions for Basic Linear Algebra
papers.abstract: We study worst-case to average-case reductions for basic linear-algebraic problems over finite fields. A seminal work of Blum, Luby, and Rubinfeld established that any algorithm that successfully multiplies more than $75\%$ of matrix pairs over any finite field, implies an algorithm with essentially the same running time multiplying any pair of matrices. A sequence of follow-ups reduced the needed fraction of successful input pairs to any positive constant. Despite most of the other basic linear algebraic operations being computationally equivalent to matrix multiplication in the worst case, no such worst-case to average-case reductions were known for them. Recently, Vaikuntanathan and Zamir introduced a cryptographic primitive called trapdoor matrices and used them to prove such worst-case to average-case reductions for matrix inversion, solving a linear system, and computing the determinant, all conditioned on common cryptographic assumptions. Our main result is the first unconditional time-preserving worst-case to average-case reduction for matrix inversion. Any algorithm that correctly inverts any constant positive fraction of uniformly random invertible matrices implies a worst-case such algorithm. We also significantly strengthen the conditional reductions based on trapdoored matrices: We establish reductions for deciding invertibility and computing rank at the optimal success thresholds, and qualitatively improve the success threshold needed in the reduction for determinant computation---while previous reductions all required the success probability to be at least $1/2$, we show that any fixed positive average-case success probability suffices for exact worst-case determinant computation over infinitely many finite fields.

papers.title: On the Convergence of Alternating Regret Matching Algorithms
papers.abstract: Alternating updates, that is, where each player is updated in turn, tend to typically perform better in regret matching algorithms than simultaneous updates. Alternation within the regret matching family has long been a central ingredient of practical solvers for zero-sum games. Yet our theoretical understanding is lagging behind. In this paper, we address this gap by developing a systematic way of analyzing such algorithms. Our framework centers on an alternating analog of the RVU property that we introduce, which we use to obtain the optimal $T^{-1}$ average-iterate convergence within this family. In particular, we establish this for two simple variants of predictive regret matching$^+$: i) increasing-regret predictive regret matching$^+$ and ii) half-prediction regret matching$^+$. Interestingly, we find that half prediction is the unique prediction multiplier that satisfies our alternating RVU property, giving it a strong theoretical justification. Going beyond average-iterate convergence, we refine our framework to obtain $T^{-1/2}$ best-iterate convergence and further establish convergence of their strategy profiles to a single Nash equilibrium, without assuming equilibrium uniqueness. We go on to establish separations between alternating and simultaneous updates, including a game in which half-prediction regret matching$^+$ converges under alternating updates but fails to converge in terms of the last iterate under simultaneous updates. This provides theoretical support for the empirical observation that alternation can stabilize learning dynamics. Finally, experiments on 15 game benchmarks demonstrate that the strong theoretical properties of the half-prediction mechanism translate to strong practical performance, being on par with state-of-the-art solvers.

papers.title: Efficient Proper Agnostic Learning of Halfspaces
papers.abstract: We give a proper membership-query algorithm for agnostically learning halfspaces under the uniform distribution on $\{\pm1\}^n$. Given query access to an arbitrary function $f:\{\pm1\}^n \to \{\pm1\}$, our algorithm runs in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)+2^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)}$ and outputs a halfspace with error at most $\mathrm{OPT}+\varepsilon$, where $\mathrm{OPT}$ is the error of the best-fitting halfspace for $f$. Previously, even with membership queries, the best known running time was $n^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)}$, achieved by the sample-based algorithm of Kalai, Klivans, Mansour, and Servedio (FOCS 2005). Our algorithm is the first agnostic halfspace learner under the uniform distribution on $\{\pm1\}^n$ whose running time is polynomial in $n$ with an exponent independent of $\varepsilon$. Combining our algorithm with a boosting argument yields a proper agnostic learner using only random examples. It achieves the same $\mathrm{OPT}+\varepsilon$ guarantee, with running time matching that of Kalai et al.\ up to an additive term depending only on $\varepsilon$. To our knowledge, this is the first sample-based proper agnostic learner in the Boolean setting with running time $2^{o(n)}$ for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$.

papers.title: ETH is Dead, Long Live SH
papers.abstract: Impagliazzo and Paturi's 1999 Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) is false, but Stearns and Hunt's 1990 Satisfiability Hypothesis (SH) remains plausible. We prove that SH is equivalent to the recently proposed Weak ETH which rules out $O(2^{n^{1-\varepsilon}})L^{O(1)}$-time 3SAT algorithms for every constant $\varepsilon>0$, where $L$ is the input length. We show that SH (or Weak ETH) preserves the typical process for lower bounds: a polynomial-time reduction from a 3SAT formula of size $s=Θ(n+m)$ to an instance of size $N\le s^{b+o(1)}$, for fixed blowup exponent $b>0$, rules out $O(2^{N^{1/b-\varepsilon}})$-time algorithms for every constant $\varepsilon>0$. By comparison, for an $N=O(s^b)$ blowup, ETH would have ruled out $2^{o(N^{1/b})}$-time algorithms. The framework also yields parameterized lower bounds ruling out running times of the form $O(2^{k^{1/b-\varepsilon}})L^{O(1)}$. We also prove equivalence of the analogous counting hypotheses, #SH and Weak #ETH, and that they rule out $O(2^{(n+m)^{1-\varepsilon}})$-time algorithms for #2SAT for every constant $\varepsilon>0$.

papers.title: Faster Exact Algorithms for 3- and 4-Coloring: Deterministic Improvements and Further Randomized Speedups
papers.abstract: We study exact exponential-time algorithms for 3- and 4-coloring. For 3-coloring, the best previously published running-time bound is $O^*(1.3289^n)$, due to Eppstein (SODA 2001). We improve this bound to $O^*(1.3204^n)$ deterministically and $O^*(1.3159^n)$ using randomization. For 4-coloring, the best previously known running-time bound is $O^*(1.7159^n)$, due to Wu, Gu, Jiang, Shao, and Xu (ESA 2024). We improve this bound to $O^*(1.6975^n)$ deterministically and $O^*(1.6933^n)$ using randomization. Our algorithms for both problems combine constraint satisfaction algorithms with dynamic programming over tree and path decompositions, exploiting their complementary strengths on different graph structures. For 6-coloring, the best published randomized running-time bound is exponentially smaller than the best published deterministic bound. For 3- and 4-coloring, however, no such improvement through randomization was previously known. To the best of our knowledge, our results provide the first randomized running-time bounds for these two problems that exponentially improve upon the best previously published deterministic bounds. This raises the question of whether randomization offers an inherent exponential advantage for 3- and 4-coloring.

papers.title: Large independent sets via neighborhood block dynamics, Glauber dynamics, and local occupancy
papers.abstract: Local occupancy can be used to bound the expected size of a hard-core independent set. The framework of locally stationary distributions shows that for triangle-free graphs, despite slow mixing at the relevant fugacity parameter, standard Glauber dynamics can be used to find sets close to the local occupancy guarantee. We improve the application of this framework to the hard-core model by replacing a conditional mixing argument with a more direct approach based on a short sequence of single-site updates that, from every initial configuration, achieves the required occupancy inequality. In general graphs, naive conditional mixing estimates or certain problematic structures in the neighborhood can in principle incur running time cost exponential in the maximum degree $Δ$. We design short update sequences that, via our relaxed criterion, yield running times polynomial in $Δ$ for graphs with a hereditary bound $b$ on the density of $K_{t,t}$ subgraphs in neighborhoods. Our methods handle the case where $t$ and $b$ can grow with the maximum degree, and the resulting algorithm attains the random graph shattering threshold when they grow sufficiently slowly. That is, we give improved local occupancy parameters and a short update sequence analysis which together show that Glauber dynamics finds independent sets of size $(1-o(1))n(\logΔ)/Δ$ in time polynomial in $n$ and $Δ$ whenever $t$ and $b$ are constant or grow suitably slowly. In a similar regime, we also establish that the (correspondence) chromatic number is at most $(1+o(1))Δ/\logΔ$ which improves upon prior results by a factor of at least $4$ in the case $t\ge 4$.

papers.title: Finding and Certifying Weighted Minimum Cuts with Cut Queries
papers.abstract: We study the deterministic and nondeterministic cut query complexity of minimum cut in undirected graphs with arbitrary nonnegative edge weights. For the nondeterministic case, we show that every $n$-vertex graph has an $O(n\log^2(2n))$-query certificate of its exact global minimum-cut value, such that any other nonnegatively weighted graph on the same vertex set that agrees on these queries has the same minimum cut value. A key ingredient is a way to certify a maximum $s$--$t$ flow value with only $O(n)$ cut queries. For the deterministic case we give an algorithm that finds an exact global minimum cut using $O(n^{3/2}\log^3(2n)(\log\log(2n))^2)$ cut queries. Previously no $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ deterministic bound was known for arbitrary nonnegatively weighted graphs. The algorithm follows Karger's two-respecting tree approach. The key new ingredient is a deterministic construction of a weak skeleton of the input graph $G$: an explicit weighted graph $H$ in which every minimum cut of $G$ is a $5/4$-approximate minimum cut.

papers.title: Information Complexity of Inner Product and Matrix Multiplication via Shannon-to-Min-Entropy Conversion
papers.abstract: We determine the information complexity of matrix multiplication over finite fields under independent uniform inputs, up to a universal additive constant. The binary inner-product case resolves the open question of Braverman, Garg, Pankratov, and Weinstein on the optimal dependence of information complexity on the error probability. For inputs in $\mathbb F_2^m$ and error at most $\varepsilon\in[0,1/2]$, the information complexity with output at Bob lies between $(1-2\varepsilon)m-c_0$ and $(1-2\varepsilon)m$, where $c_0<4.772$ is a universal constant. For independent uniform matrices $X\in\mathbb F_q^{t\times m}$ and $Y\in\mathbb F_q^{s\times m}$, where $t\le s$, computing $XY^{\mathsf T}$ with output at Bob and error at most $\varepsilon\in[0,1]$ has information complexity $(1-q^{ts}\varepsilon/(q^{ts}-1))^+mt\log_2q$, up to an additive gap of less than $9.544$ bits. This gap is independent of the matrix dimensions, field size, and error. At zero error, the information complexity is exactly $mt\log_2q$. The information lower bounds for both inner product and matrix multiplication follow from a new Shannon-to-min-entropy theorem for convolution on discrete groups. Let $Q_1,\ldots,Q_k$ be the finitely supported distributions of independent random variables taking values in a discrete group, and let $s$ be the largest support size. We show that if $k\ge\lceil\lfloor\log_2s\rfloor\ln2\rceil$, then the min-entropy of their ordered product is at least the average Shannon entropy of the $Q_i$ minus $c_0$ bits. This holds for arbitrary discrete groups, including infinite and noncommutative groups, even when the input distributions differ. The leading coefficient of the logarithmic threshold is optimal.

papers.title: Full-Rank Constructions of Explicit Lossless Expanders and Good Small-Set qLTCs
papers.abstract: We construct explicit two-sided lossless expanders whose binary adjacency matrices have full rank, and use them to obtain explicit asymptotically good quantum LDPC codes whose specified X- and Z-check matrices have full row rank and satisfy small-set soundness, or confinement, on a linear range. Our lossless expanders are a variant of those of Hsieh, Lubotzky, Mohanty, Reiner, and Zhang, with a free action of a finite 2-group. Under such an action, injectivity and surjectivity of the adjacency matrix are detected on a fixed-size matrix indexed by vertex orbits. Adding a sparse factor to the gadget at the middle vertices of a single type then enforces full rank, with a controlled loss in expansion. To obtain the 2-group action, we observe that reducing the generators of the Lubotzky-Phillips-Sarnak Ramanujan graphs modulo powers of 2, instead of modulo an odd prime, gives Ramanujan Cayley graphs on finite 2-groups. This construction may be of independent interest. Plugging two such expanders into the balanced product of Lin and Hsieh gives the quantum codes, since full rank of the input graphs is inherited by the check matrices. Our construction supplies the code family sought by Hong, Guo, and Lucas. Applying their analysis, within their framework and under their dynamical assumptions, gives quantum memories whose free-energy density is analytic at every positive temperature and whose guaranteed lifetime is $exp(Ω(N))$ at sufficiently low fixed positive temperature, where N is the blocklength. This improves the previously guaranteed stretched-exponential timescale.

papers.title: Counting Feedback Vertex Sets of All Sizes in Subexponential Time, Conditionally
papers.abstract: Assuming a Boolean tensor contraction hypothesis (Theorem D.1 of OpenAI's recent preprint refuting the Exponential Time Hypothesis), we study exact feedback vertex set counting in general graphs. For an $n$-vertex, $m$-edge simple graph, we compute the complete size distribution deterministically in $\mathrm{poly}(n+m)\,2^{O(n(\log\log n)^2/\sqrt{\log n})}$ time and polynomial working space. The algorithm combines a whole-edge forest identity, subset-index scalar networks, sparse parity filtering, and disjoint high-degree branching. A binomial inversion recovers the multiplicities introduced by exceptional-set guesses. The counting interface supports fixed vertices, minimum solutions, and unranking. Component markers yield induced-tree and induced-path counts within the same bound. Sparse Hamilton, forest, and Steiner edge-tree counting follow from the scalar encoding.

papers.title: DisC: Incentive Design for Green, Robust, and Fair Client Self-Participation in OTA Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Over-the-Air Federated Learning (OTA-FL) improves communication efficiency by exploiting waveform superposition over wireless Multiple-Access Channels (MAC). However, client heterogeneity, fading, energy constraints, and participation imbalance can degrade both fairness and aggregation accuracy. Existing Pareto-oriented fair OTA-FL schemes may still suffer from large aggregation distortion when highly weighted clients experience poor channel conditions. This paper proposes DisC, a game-theoretic distributed client selection framework for fairness-aware, channel-aware, and energy-efficient OTA-FL. Each client selects its participation level by maximizing a utility that captures Pareto fairness importance, learning relevance, OTA distortion, energy consumption, and delay. We show that DisC admits a Nash equilibrium and can be formulated as an exact potential game, where stable equilibria correspond to locally optimal OTA-FL operating points. DisC therefore offers a distributed, incentive-compatible alternative to centralized client selection under wireless and resource constraints.
papers.comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE GLOBECOM 2026

papers.title: Submodularity Is Barely Testable
papers.abstract: In 2010, Seshadhri and Vondrák asked: is submodularity testable? For functions $f : \{ 0, 1 \}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, they gave a tester that makes $2^{O(\sqrt{n} \log n)}$ queries. We show that every tester, even an adaptive one with two-sided error, must make $2^{Ω(\sqrt{n})}$ queries, thereby concluding: submodularity is barely testable.

papers.title: Circuit Lower Bounds for Extended Gate Bases from Subexponential Counting
papers.abstract: We study circuit lower bounds for extended gate bases using exact CNF counting and an extension-ring form of the contraction theorem of OpenAI. The deterministic counting theorem of Claude (Anthropic) yields an $\mathsf{E}^{\mathsf{NP}}$ language requiring $Ω(m\sqrt{\log m}/\log\log m)$ gates over unbounded AND/OR with binary XOR, infinitely often. Using that contraction theorem, a bounded binary base with a linear budget of arbitrary XOR and symmetric gates requires $Ω(m\sqrt{\log m})$ gates infinitely often. These results extend the binary-gate lower bound of OpenAI. Signed long-clause selectors reduce the first counting problem to the difference of two ordinary 3-CNF counts. Affine characters and unit-separated interpolation give the second counting interface, with logarithmic cost per symmetric-gate arity. A quantitative local-reduction transfer accounts for auxiliary variables, branch counts, and integer recovery.

papers.title: Generalized Flows over Time: Complexity, Structure and Algorithm
papers.abstract: Generalized flows over time constitute a general network flow model that incorporates both transit times and flow losses or gains. We study their complexity, structure, and approximation. We prove that the generalized maximum flow over time problem remains NP-hard under standard binary encoding, even on lossy two-terminal series-parallel networks. The maximum temporally repeated restriction is APX-hard with general gains and NP-hard on lossy networks. We then consider the minimum source supply needed to satisfy a fixed sink demand within a given horizon, and prove that an optimal solution always exists without intermediate storage. On lossy networks, such a solution can additionally use only simple source--sink paths. These structural properties yield a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme via time condensation, with analogous schemes for generalized maximum flows over time and quickest flows with a source-supply budget.

papers.title: Iterated Narrow Networks: Turing Completeness at Width 4 on Convex Input Spaces and the Complexity of Verification
papers.abstract: We study the iterates of a fixed ReLU network $N$ of width 4, that is, the discrete-time system $x_{k+1} = N(x_k)$ on $[0,1]^4$. Equivalently, $x_k$ is the output of a weight-tied network made of $k$ copies of $N$, or of a recurrent network with no external input, started at $x_0$. We prove that every deterministic Turing machine $M$ admits such a network $N_M$. The network can be constructed in polynomial time from $M$. Each iteration has depth $\mathrm{poly}(|M|)$. The iterates of $N_M$ simulate $M$ exactly on every encoded tape. The number of iterations is proportional to the running time of $M$. Moreover, the fourth coordinate irreversibly flags every point of the convex cube $[0,1]^4$ whose simulation reads an invalid digit. This flag is the certificate that makes hardness reductions sound on convex input regions, the regime of practical verifiers. Convex regions were previously inaccessible because of a continuity obstruction inherent to ReLU networks. The correspondence has three consequences. First, reachability for iterated width-4 ReLU networks spans the full complexity hierarchy along the single axis of the time bound: it is NP-complete for a unary bound, NEXP-complete for a binary bound and RE-complete (undecidable) with no bound. Second, two extra neurons of width suffice to extend the hardness to every common smooth activation: at width 6, the robust verification problem (a promise problem with $δ/2δ$ gap) is NP-complete for $\tanh$, sigmoid, GELU, Swish, ELU, and any polynomial-time-computable continuous non-polynomial activation with a polynomial-time-computable Lipschitz constant. Third, the whole spectrum transfers to discretized Neural ODEs in dimension 5.

papers.title: Pair-Relative Partial Equivariance for Rotation-Robust Keypoint Descriptor Matching
papers.abstract: Learned keypoint descriptors trained on upright imagery often fail under large in-plane rotation. Steerers address this by applying a single exact SO(2) representation to the descriptor space, but this global group constraint can be too rigid for keypoint descriptors, whose angular responses need not follow a single group representation. We propose pair-relative partial equivariance, which measures equivariance under the empirical distribution of relative rotations in image pairs, and PaSteer, a relaxed descriptor-steering framework that allows the steering map to leave the exact representation manifold while retaining the lightweight, backbone-free design of steering. PaSteer instantiates this relaxation with two variants: an identity-preserving residual steerer (PaSteer-soft) and a free-form Fourier steerer (PaSteer-free). We show that the per-angle optimal linear steerer for a fixed non-equivariant descriptor generally does not obey the group composition law, explaining why exact representations can be suboptimal in the frozen-descriptor regime. On Roto-360, MegaDepth-1500, AIMS, and IMC-PT, PaSteer consistently improves rotation-robust matching over an exact steerer on frozen DeDoDe descriptors, especially under large relative rotations, with minimal upright degradation.

papers.title: Exponential Lower Bounds for Products of Cubic Polynomials over Prime Fields
papers.abstract: We study exact representations of explicit signed modular predicates on $\{-1,1\}^n$ as products of bounded-degree polynomials over prime fields, measured by total variable-occurrence cost. Our main result is an exponential lower bound for products of cubic polynomials. Over $\mathbb F_3$ the proof is self-contained: every cubic factor in a nonvanishing product is a unit on the sign cube, the unit identity forces bounded affine-observation complexity, and a simultaneous clustering argument converts this structural compression into an exponential occurrence lower bound. We also give an alternative reconstruction route that isolates the quadratic structure behind the cubic classification. We then extend the cubic theorem to every fixed prime field $\mathbb F_p$ of characteristic greater than three for odd target modulus $q$ coprime to $p$. The only non-elementary structural input in this extension is Karam's restricted-range rank theorem; the conversion from multiplication to parity and the $p$-tuple clustering argument are proved explicitly. Finally, we establish a coefficient-field-independent degree-lifting principle. If a lower bound is known at one fixed degree, restriction to a large independent set yields a quantitative lower bound at the next degree. In particular, the exponential cubic theorem implies $ L^{(p,q)}_4(n)=Ω_{p,q}\!\left(\frac{n^4}{(\log(2+n))^3}\right). $ For the characteristic-three core this already gives a lower bound for a restricted mixed-modulus circuit class.

papers.title: Persuasion by Parts
papers.abstract: Classical Bayesian persuasion assumes that an information designer can condition signals on the entire state. We propose persuasion by parts. In this model, the receiver's payoff from acting is $X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ for independent coordinates $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ observed by separate sources. The designer commits in advance to a product experiment, in which each source $i$ can condition its signal only on $X_i$. Given the signals, the receiver computes her posterior mean $y$ of $X$ and acts with probability $g(y)$, where $g\colon \mathbb{R} \to [0,1]$ is a nondecreasing function. The designer aims to maximize the probability of action. Let $V_{\mathrm{prod}}(g)$ and $V_{\mathrm{joint}}(g)$ be the supremum probabilities of action under persuasion by parts and under joint persuasion, respectively. When the designer knows $g$, we show $$ V_{\mathrm{prod}}(g) \;\ge\; c\,V_{\mathrm{joint}}(g)^2 \qquad\text{for every nondecreasing } g\colon \mathbb{R} \to [0,1], $$ where $c > 0$ is an absolute constant independent of $n$ and the prior; the exponent $2$ is tight. When $g$ is unknown, we construct a product experiment $Π$ from the prior alone, whose probability of action $V_Π(g)$ satisfies $$ V_Π(g) \;\ge\; c_\varepsilon\,V_{\mathrm{joint}}(g)^{2 + \varepsilon} \qquad\text{for every } \varepsilon > 0 \text{ and every nondecreasing } g\colon \mathbb{R} \to [0,1], $$ where $c_\varepsilon > 0$ depends only on $\varepsilon$.

papers.title: Sketching in Regression: Sketchy in Practice?
papers.abstract: The Johnson-Lindenstrauss (JL) lemma and its extensions provide tools for solving the $L_2$ regression problem in high-dimensional settings with $n>d$, by transforming a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$, (where $m<n$) while approximately preserving the norms of elements of the subspace. In this paper, we study the theoretical guarantees made by various JL-based subspace embeddings critically and concretely to gauge their practical applicability. We derive concrete versions of results on subspace embeddings in the literature to establish lower bounds on the reduced dimension as well as to concretely analyze the complexity of the Fast JL, OSNAP Transforms among other embeddings. These analyses suggest that guaranteeing substantial computational savings while maintaining the accuracy of the sketched solution requires data dimensions larger than those typically encountered in practice. We also see that, for practically necessary accuracy requirements or for sparsity requirements for computational gain, existing theoretical guarantees lead to substantially large reduced dimensions. This leads to very stringent data requirements for establishing guarantees of any kind.

papers.title: Dynamic Coalition Formation Under Capacity Constraints: A Regime-Switching Value-Investing Game
papers.abstract: Edge computing service deployment requires the Network Operator (NO) and Service Providers (SPs) to coordinate investment and resource allocation under uncertain demand. This paper develops an audit-based service management framework for daily coalition formation with fixed capacity and service-level agreement (SLA) reservations. A two-stage coalitional game separates infrastructure investment from operational participation. Demand follows a Geometric Random Walk (GRW), and SPs apply an ordered admission and suspension rule using reported marginal contributions. With the NO held fixed, the operational coalition value is submodular; mandatory reservations can produce negative Shapley payoffs. We derive a separable benchmark, compute operational Shapley allocations, and give a sufficient condition for convergence to an individual equilibrium. A probabilistic audit mechanism provides a conditional daily truthfulness guarantee under verified settlement and enforceable penalties. For five service classes over three years, the reference run gains 12.4% over static grand-coalition membership and recovers 94.6% of the full-information optimum. Across 30 runs, the median gain is 13.3%. Sensitivity tests examine policy parameters, capacity and alternative demand models. The gain depends on capacity and update order; abundant capacity can make the admission rule underperform static membership.

papers.title: Pointwise Score Evaluation from Succinct Boolean Descriptions: SAT Equivalence for Strongly Log-Concave Gaussian Mixtures
papers.abstract: Score-based generative models rely on access to accurate scores, but the cost of computing those scores depends on how the underlying distribution is represented. Can smoothness and strong log-concavity make score evaluation efficient when a distribution is specified by Boolean constraints? I investigate this question by separating geometric encoding from computational extraction. I construct a succinctly specified Gaussian mixture whose score at a fixed query location encodes whether a Boolean formula is satisfiable. The construction has rational component means and uniform strong log-concavity, yet deterministic polynomial-time approximation of the designated score coordinate to constant absolute accuracy is equivalent to polynomial-time solvability of Boolean satisfiability. This equivalence remains valid throughout a neighborhood whose radius is independent of dimension. I further characterize how numerical precision connects bounded witness enumeration to exact counting, and show that independent sample access turns the same target into a dimension-independent mean-estimation problem. An explicit parity construction also separates low-degree approximation from efficient computation. Together, these results show that favorable geometry alone does not resolve the computational cost of extracting scores from compact descriptions. They identify the precise extraction requirement in this formulation while leaving the existence of a general efficient evaluator open.

papers.title: A Cooperative Game-Theoretic Framework for Real-Time Deviation Settlement in Local Energy Communities
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a cooperative game-theoretical framework for the financial settlement of real-time deviations in Community-Based Local Energy Markets (CB-LEMs). The real-time settlement process is modeled as a transferable-utility cooperative game, and the resulting Real-Time Local Energy Market (RTLEM) game is shown to be superadditive and balanced. We analyze two game-theoretical allocation mechanisms, the Shapley value and the nucleolus, and evaluate their efficiency, individual rationality, coalitional rationality, and temporal-aggregation properties. We subsequently compare these mechanisms with a settlement rule based on proportional imbalance responsibility. The three mechanisms are efficient and individually rational, but only the nucleolus is guaranteed to satisfy coalitional rationality for every RTLEM instance. The proposed framework is demonstrated using real-world data from a residential energy community in Amsterdam, showing the trade-offs among the three allocation mechanisms in terms of surplus distribution, coalitional stability, interpretability, and computational requirements.

papers.title: Non-simple Arrangements of Lines and Pseudolines with Many Triangles
papers.abstract: We study affine arrangements of an even number $n$ of lines and pseudolines with many triangles. For simple ones, Blanc's bound limits the number of triangular faces to $\lfloor n(n-5/2)/3\rfloor$. Adapting the Bartholdi-Blanc-Loisel doubling to the even case, we construct an infinite series of arrangements of $n=6\cdot2^t+2$ ($8,14,26,50,\ldots$) straight lines with two triple points and $(n(n-5/2)+1)/3$ triangles, one more than the simple bound allows. We obtain exhaustive enumerations of triangle-maximal pseudoline arrangements, simple or not, for even $n\le12$. For $n=6,8,10,12,14$ the maximum number of triangles, for both lines and pseudolines, is $7,15,25,38,54$; for $n=8,12,14$ every optimal arrangement has multiple points. All optimal arrangements for even $n\le12$ are realizable by straight lines, except two arrangements of 10 pseudolines, which are not stretchable. For the odd value $n=11$, no arrangement with $33$ triangles exists even with multiple points. We also obtain even arrangements by adding a line to odd ones. For $n\equiv2\pmod 6$ this again gives one triangle more than the simple bound, in pseudolines up to $n=44$ and in straight lines for $n=20$ and $n=32$. Doubling these pseudoline arrangements gives members of the series $18\cdot2^t+2$ and $30\cdot2^t+2$ with the same excess, up to $n=146$ and $n=242$, respectively; those with $n=38$ and $n=74$ are realizable by straight lines. These results lead us to conjecture that an arrangement of an even number $n$ of pseudolines has at most $\lfloor n(n-2)/3\rfloor-\lfloor n/6\rfloor$ triangles.
papers.comment: 72 pages, 19 figures, 8 tables. Code, enumeration outputs and certificates: https://github.com/parpalak/nonsimple-arrangements

papers.title: Revisiting (Bijective) Burrows-Wheeler Transform Space-Time Trade-Off Constructions
papers.abstract: The bijective Burrows-Wheeler transform (BBWT) replaces the delimiter of the ordinary BWT by a Lyndon factorization and sorts factor conjugates in $ω$-order. It admits quadratic-time constant-workspace algorithms and linear-time linear-space algorithms. We extend the small-space BWT trade-off of Crochemore et al. [JDA,'15] to the BBWT and accelerate both constructions. For $τ\in [3..n]$, let $σ_τ\le\min(σ,τ+1)$ be the maximum construction-batch alphabet size. We construct either transform in $ O\!\left( \frac{n^2}τ \frac{\logτ}{\log\logτ} \right) $ time and $O(τσ_τ)$ additional space, assuming $τσ_τ=O(n)$. This improves the transferred $O((n^2/τ)\logτ)$ bound by a $\log\logτ$ factor. If $σ_τ\in w^{O(1)}$, where $w\inΩ(\log n)$ is the word size, the time improves to $ O\!\left( \frac{n^2}τ + \frac{n\logτ}{\log\logτ} \right). $ For inversion, the same bounds hold with the global alphabet size $σ$ in place of $σ_τ$.

papers.title: State Synthesis with an NP oracle
papers.abstract: In this note, I describe a quantum algorithm that prepares an arbitrary state $|ψ\rangle$ to inverse exponential precision in polynomial time by making queries to an $\mathsf{NP}$ oracle, assuming one can directly query entries of the state vector corresponding to $|ψ\rangle$. The previous best upper bound on the complexity class required by an oracle for this task was $\mathsf{PP}$. I provide evidence that $\mathsf{NP}$ is the best possible upper bound by showing that any quantum algorithm using a $\mathsf{P}$ oracle, or even a $\mathsf{P/poly}$ oracle, requires exponentially many queries. I also discuss some implications of this result for the $\mathsf{QMA}$ search-to-decision problem and unitary synthesis.

papers.title: Coalitions, Stability, and Majority Jackpots: Frameworks for Unifying Majoritarian and Proportional Allocation in Multiwinner Elections
papers.abstract: Social choice literature on multiwinner elections tends to focus on characterizing two distinct tasks: majoritarian representation and proportional representation. However, many real world systems can be viewed as operating between these two extremes, such as majority jackpot systems used in several countries throughout history. Towards the goal of better understanding these systems from a social choice perspective, we introduce two frameworks that encompass existing desiderata for majoritarian and proportional settings: coalitions, which encompasses properties such as fixed majority and solid coalitions; and stability, which encompasses various generalizations of Condorcet's criterion for single-winner elections, such as Gehrlein stability and local stability, among others. We develop theory and tools that characterize the mathematical and computational aspects of both frameworks across a wide array of preference structures (such as the unrestricted domain over candidates and the restricted domain of party lists). Building on this foundation, we shed new light on majority jackpot electoral systems, which to date have received limited mathematical analysis in the social choice literature.

papers.title: Classification Aggregation with Multiple Memberships
papers.abstract: People face the problem of classifying objects into categories while aggregating their opinions. We axiomatically study such a classification aggregation problem with multiple memberships, meaning that each individual assigns one category to every object, whereas the resulting classification may assign more than one category. Under the natural settings and axioms (i.e., Independence and Supportiveness), each of our new axioms -- Responsibility, Split Stability and Rejection Stability -- characterises what we call the junta rules. The rules assign a category to an object exactly when some member of a fixed coalition does so. The coalitions that can secure an assignment form a grill, a topological structure implied by an ultrafilter. Hence, the study parallels the literature on Arrow's theorem characterised by the decisive coalition structures. An infinite population setting is also investigated to clarify the differences among the axioms.
